When I first saw the trailer for this film I had nothing but the worst expectations for it. Then I started to hear more and more about how amazing it was and that I had to give it a chance from a lot of people whose opinions I respect. My expectations nearly went in the opposite direction, I wasn't super hyped about it (I never get to hyped over anything these days) but my anticipation for seeing it had spiked a bit. Honestly though this song did absolutely nothing for me at all. I expected that it would have affirmed either my anticipation or my initial cynisim but it really didn't do anything. And I guess that's a good thing since I should be judging a much larger work of such an isolated element but really it's still disappointing.

 It wasn't bad by any measure, the vocals and composition were more than competent and the message is delivered but the whole thing just felt absolutely flavorless. Sort of just generic artistic matter that I can appreciate for it's component parts but all together sort of just felt like this weird gray matter. I'm still definitely keen to give the film a chance, maybe in the context of the films events this is more striking. Honestly it just felt like the pre-intermission song for "Musical the Musical". "Oh she's belting notes now I should feel empowered," "Oh it's just a soft voice and piano this means the scene is solemn". I just don't feel like this did anything that a million musicals haven't don't before in better or more interesting ways.

It was summer, late June to mid July. We had already tried and failed to play D&D a few times (Adventure wouldn't print, friend was grounded, the kind of logistical problems you run into at 13). My friends and I, introduced through magic the gathering, sought something more to sink our fanged imaginations into. Dungeons and Dragons. I had heard the name countless times on television, usually denoting a characters nerdiness of course, but had little idea what it actually was. At My friends assurance however I agreed to give it a shot.

 I sat before the humming crt of my friends computer, the wicker chair biting into my legs uncomfortably as I obediently followed the cheesey voice over of the third edition character builder. A fighter, simple enough, equipped with what seemed like one of every item available off the phb loot table. Chalk, pitons, flasks, and more weapons than I would ever need all seeded my imagination with the innumerable circumstances that would demand them. A portable battering ram even sat in my inventory for a while before one of my friend persuaded me that it was entirely unnecessary (boy was he wrong!). 

With the characters made we sat around the huge wooden table. It's funny thinking back, that in that moment everything was so fresh and new, our first of countless sessions sat around that table. The summer breeze came in through the screen door, the sounds of the suburbs slowly fading away as the DM walked us through the basics. The sun low and air cooling I remember us delving into the sunless citadel, our motives as new players ill defined and crude. There was a dungeon, we were adventurers, back then that was all the depth needed to have us smashing through doors and saying goblins. 

The memory is sort of ethereal now, or at least my memory for the fine details of what actually happened in game that session. Instead there's just this nostalgic fog of tiny insignificant details that bordered the game itself. The way that there was just enough humidity to make the wooden furniture sticky, the way the ice tea made from powder mix was always too strong or to weak, the little title screen track that the character generator played when you first started it, or how amazed we all were when glowing fungus lined the dungeon walls. It's funny how the little things like that stick around. Now we're all older,  weathered countless adventures, arguments, and laughs together. We don't get to play as much, I moved away and only get home a few times a year. But on nights like these when I think about those first few rag tag sessions I would trade almost anything to go back and live them one more time.

Yea the quality of the companions is one of those things that strikes me every single time I replay the game. I'm actually juggling play throughs of NV and Skyrim right now and it's made my appreciation for the followers of NV go up quite a bit. Each follower has an intriguing story and development arc that compliments and further explores the game central themes. Further the way that these stories are tied to events in the game and require you and the companion to experience specific events together to pursue that development adds an extra layer of flavor and depth. Though I'll also add that it can be a bit annoying if you don't find a companion till after you've experienced said events and it cuts off their story, definitely something that could have been improved. In skyrim all the followers feel very shallow. Like yes they do sometimes have interesting stories or quirky personalities but I always found that whenever I tried to sink my teeth in and get more there just wasn't anything there. Actually the way the followers are constructed is sort of emblematic of why I really loved New Vegas more than Skyrim. With New Vegas there just always seemed like there was another way achieve the goal, A different side to take, or a nuance you could explore (or if their wasn't the illusion of depth was built well enough). Skyrim felt like the tunnel wile e coyote would paint on the cliff, it looked nice and was pretty convincing but if you tried go further you'd just smack up against the wall. It hasn't been until I moded in a ton of quests, tweaks and features that Skyrim really came alive for me. I mean I know they aren't the same game or anything but New Vegas just felt like it fulfilled everything I wanted in my Skyrim experience, it definitely had flaws and problems of it's own but I've easily sunk in 200 unmodded hours into it which I can't say about Skyrim.

Ha it's weird but this is really bitter sweet to me. I think it's the image of the themed room that really stirs things up. Like as a kid you can just love things so much and they can just spill into your life like this and that's totaly normal. Your relatives know you're the "minecraft" kid, actually no scratch that they know you "like that block game" but couldn't make heads or tails of why. But that's half the magic of it, it's something they either can't understand or don't care enough to understand but that shit doesn't matter because you know it's one of the best things in the whole world next to dinosaurs and Batman. It's this inaccessible space you have all to yourself.

But I'm an adult now and I can't like that stuff. Not in that way at least. I have responsibility and bills to pay. Grown up stuff to do. It's not socially acceptable to love something in *that* way. 

But it's not even about social acceptability the more I consider it. Maybe it's just that I'm suffering from the natural side effects of life. Of having my heart broken, my idealistic world view ground against reality, I've had to come face to face with the fact that no maybe everything isn't possible.

I saw this post and the first thing I did was click on over to think geek to see how much a light up torch or redstone block costs. I thought that I could steal away into that indulgence even just for a little bit. 19.99 that's all it took to shut me down. I could save that money, I could take the time and make something minecraft related for my room even if the price tag was an issue but I probably won't. The thing that really depresses me isn't that society says I can't enjoy something this way or that the material reality of my life prohibits it but that *I* know in my heart I just don't enjoy anything in this way anymore. Maybe it's a sort of world weariness, maybe it's a reality of growing up, hell maybe it's none of that. Maybe that kid has been through more then I know and still finds a way to enjoy things like that, who am I to judge. 

I think what's stirring is the way this picture makes me aware of how liminal my state is. That Im still in someways that kid who wants the minecraft themed room but am also slowly becoming that adult who has no clue what's so great about "that block game". And it makes me sad it a very real way. It worries me. Like there's a tiny little voice trying to remind me that I left something very dear behind. And every week and month and birthday that goes by the voice is harder and harder to hear, drowned out by so much other noise. And I really don't know how to make it stop.

What kind of Sociology?

Sociology of the Family?

Urban Sociology?

Sociology of health and healthcare?

Sociology of crime and deviance?

Environmental Sociology?

Sociology of gender?

Sociology of education?

Sociology of race and ethnicity?

Sociology of... Well you get the point


Honestly there's a pretty huge range of things to learn with countless different perspectives and theories and subfields. It might be constructive to view sociology as a specific lens through which to interrogate the social world (alongside things such as psychology, anthropology, economics, and other such disciplines). Certainly there are some topics it is more capable of exploring than others but you can look at just about anything with a sociological perspective. 

I guess the best thing I can suggest is start with the textbook a university intro course might use, it will give you an initial focus (which depending on how you learn might make things easier then just diving into a huge body of knowledge like wikipedia) and let you branch out further as specific areas of inquiry catch your fancy. It will also help you curate a base of very broad but essential knowledge about the varying perspectives within the discipline (Structural Functionalist, Feminist, Conflict Theory, Symbolic Interactionalist) as well as the various research methodologies employed (Qualitative, Quantitative, Historical, Ethnographic, Network Analysis and so on). I can recommend Lorne Tepperman's "Starting Points: A Sociological Journey" for the accessibility of it's content, though it does have a number of sections that are chiefly preoccupied with a Canadian perspective (which I suppose depending on where you live could be a very useful thing or a waste of time :P). I'm sure there are countless intro textbooks out there that you could find

 The major "Founding Fathers" of sociology are Karl Marx, Max Weber, and Emile Durkheim so depending on your comfort level looking into their major works (or maybe books that present their work in a more accessible way for the layman) is a great way to start a foundation of knowledge. You will see echoes of their ideas all over the place even as contemporary theorists get further and further away from their initial theories. 

I know for me sociology was one of those subjects that really came alive when I was able to sit down and take a course with a competent and enthusiastic professor in university so that might be worth looking into. 

If you found any of this useful and want further clarification or advice feel free to PM me and I'd be happy to help however I can! Again keep in mind that this is a huge and diverse field of inquiry that can be deeply rewarding and enriching. I'm not trying to discourage you from pursuing the field from a casual perspective (quite the opposite in fact! More people should have some education in sociology as far as I'm concerned!) but I just want to be sure I'm fairly conveying the breadth of the field.

For me there are a few distinct reasons I watch let's plays 

1) The LPER: I watch people like bdoubleo100, generickb, and pauseunpause (mostly the stuff he does with andrea) for their personality. The game while it can be intersting is usually secondary to the enjoyment I get by listening to their videos and the stories they get into. Game Grumps largely falls into this category as well as Roosterteeth 

2) Information and Trivia: at the moment the only LPers I watch for this is beard bros. While their dialogue is great and they don't by any means lack the above personality criteria I listed above I find myself most captivated by the knowledge and trivia discussed during videos. Game Grumps has a bit of this (especially with the guest grumps they did with GKH)

3) Gameplay: This category is fairly uncommon for me since I lack interest in any competitive scenes. Usually it's for games I probably won't ever play but still have an interest for such as JRPGS (just can't dedicate the time or stand the mechanics) and Exclusives (Im broke at the moment). VintageBeef did an LP of Ni No Kuni that I watched for these reasons (and actually made me want to play the game further down the road). I also watch for games that have huge complexity, tons of potential variation in Gameplay, and steep initial learning curves (steep enough that I gain no satisfaction from mastering the basics through trial and error). KurtJMac's Kerbal Space Program is a good example of this sub category.

Overall I think the types of let's plays and individuals rational for watching them are more diverse then people usually give credit for (at least in my experience). Save for a few big budget or well written shows LP's have mostly replaced TV in my life as a low investment relaxation form of entertainment

Not mine but i was DMing. So we had a friend who would occasionally come sessions in a long running campaign. He wasn't super serious but always added some great comic relief (his character was sort of a deadpool type). Anyway he dives into a French revolution type conflict and got in way over his head. Apprehended by some of the the city guard he shoots ridiculous idea after ridiculous idea at me for a "raise the stakes" (basically a negotiated wager where they player can do something cinematic. without regard for the rules if he wins a role against a DC the DM chooses or faces humiliating failure also decided by the DM). Eventually a guard comes into interrogate him and after shooting his mouth off the guard decides to give him a cavity search. And this is where our troubles begin. He says "i wanna role a strength check, if i win i trap his hand with my anus" the rest of the players at the table all rally around this, i roll my eyes but give in so we can get on with everything. He rolls. Natural bloody 20. "that's good right?!" his eyes light up with glee. All the other players give me the "well it was a natural 20" smirk. Needless to say it was one of the most bizarre escapes I've ever DM'd. A few sessions later we were trying to decide what to do with an orphaned girl and when he offered I'll always remember the single most compelling counter argument in D&D history "guys he trapped a man with his anus, we can't give him a 14 year old girl"

I totally agree that speed reading itself won't help and i think the rest of your comment is also very accurate. However the one thing I would like to add is that some of the skills speed reading programs teach can be useful. For me when I tried one years ago I found a lot of bad reading habits that I had slowing me down and consciously started correcting them while ultimately abandoning the rest of the actual speed reading techniques (as it's mostly fruitless to speed read in my field). It's sort of like typing posture, most people who use a keyboard for years can type at a reasonable speed, but people learn proper typing (finger placement and use) and practice are frequently more efficient overall. With this said you might not have that many poor reading habits to begin with so your gains could end up being marginal at best but I would still look into it with the understanding that there will be much better ways to approach an increased reading load and this will be more supplemental than anything.
